body:
Meaning of folk music

Folk music is the traditional music that develops within a community and reflects its language, customs, beliefs, occupations, environment and everyday experiences. It forms an important part of the cultural heritage of rural, tribal and other regional communities.

Folk music is closely connected with the occasions on which it is performed. Agricultural communities sing during sowing and harvesting, families sing during marriages and childbirth ceremonies, and communities come together to sing during festivals and religious gatherings. The words and melodies often reflect the experiences of the people who preserve them.

Principal characteristics

  • Regional identity: Folk songs commonly use local languages and dialects.
  • Oral transmission: Songs are frequently learned through listening, imitation and repeated performance rather than through written notation.
  • Collective participation: Many forms encourage participation by families or communities.
  • Connection with everyday life: Subjects include agriculture, occupations, marriage, separation, seasonal changes, religious faith and historical events.
  • Variation: The words and melodies of a traditional song may differ between villages, communities and generations.
  • Traditional instruments: Locally familiar instruments such as the ektara, dholak, flute and manjira often accompany singing.

Meaning of devotional music

Devotional music is music performed primarily to express religious faith, spiritual love, worship or remembrance of the divine. It may communicate religious teachings, describe the deeds of a deity, express surrender or encourage ethical conduct.

Bhajan, kirtan, abhang, shabad kirtan and qawwali are important examples of devotional musical traditions in the Indian subcontinent.

Relationship between folk, devotional and classical music

CategoryPrincipal basisExamples
Folk musicCommunity tradition and regional cultural lifePanihari, Bhatiali, Gujarati wedding songs
Devotional musicReligious or spiritual purposeBhajan, kirtan, qawwali
Classical musicEstablished musical systems and conventionsHindustani and Carnatic music

These categories are not mutually exclusive. A devotional composition may be sung using a folk melody or a classical raga. Similarly, a folk tradition may have both religious and non-religious purposes.

For example, Gujarati Garba songs traditionally praise the goddess during Navaratri. They belong to a regional folk tradition while also serving a devotional purpose. In contrast, a traditional wedding song may be primarily social rather than devotional.

Distinguish the basis of classification

Folk music is identified primarily by its cultural setting and transmission, whereas devotional music is identified primarily by its religious or spiritual purpose. Classical music is identified by its established musical system. A single composition can belong to more than one of these categories.

Music as part of other performing arts

Music frequently accompanies traditional dance, theatre, storytelling and ritual. Garba and Raas combine music with dance, while Bhavai incorporates music into folk theatre. Therefore, the presence of singing does not necessarily mean that a tradition is exclusively a musical genre.

Prelims focus

  • Oral transmission and regional identity are important characteristics of folk music.
  • Devotional music is classified principally by its spiritual purpose.
  • Hindustani and Carnatic are the major Indian classical music systems.
  • Garba illustrates the overlap between folk and devotional traditions.
  • Trap: Folk music need not be anonymous, exclusively rural or entirely non-religious.

[References: NCERT, Living Craft Traditions of India, Class 11, Chapter 10, Theatre Crafts, pp. 113, 117–121; NCERT, Our Pasts-II, Class 7, 2020–21, Chapter 8, pp. 104–115; Centre for Cultural Resources and Training, Performing Arts; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Social Science, Standard 10, English edition, Chapter 2, p. 12; online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Music as a living community tradition.

title: Nature and Characteristics of Folk and Devotional Music

body:
Regional diversity

India's folk music traditions reflect differences in climate, occupations, historical experiences and social customs. A song associated with the monsoon in one region may differ considerably from a song associated with water collection in a desert region.

Regional associations identify the areas in which a musical tradition is particularly prominent. They do not necessarily establish exclusive geographical boundaries because communities, languages and musical traditions extend across state borders.

Rajasthan and Kashmir

FormRegionDistinctive feature
MaandRajasthanExpressive songs of love, separation and regional life
PanihariRajasthanWomen's songs associated with fetching water
WanawanKashmirTraditional ceremonial songs, particularly weddings
ChakriKashmirPopular traditional group singing

Panihari and the desert environment

The word Panihari refers to a woman who collects or carries water. Panihari songs reflect the importance of water in Rajasthan's dry environment. They also express domestic experiences, affection and separation. The association between these songs and water collection makes them an important example of occupational and environmental influence on folk music.

Maand

Maand is a distinctive Rajasthani singing tradition noted for its expressive melodies. It has developed through interaction between regional folk music and more structured musical traditions. Kesariya Balam is a well-known song associated with Maand.

Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and Punjab

FormPrincipal regionTheme or occasion
Kajri or KajariEastern Uttar Pradesh and BiharMonsoon, longing and separation
ChaitiUttar Pradesh and BiharSpring and the Hindu month of Chaitra
SoharUttar Pradesh and BiharCelebration of childbirth
RasiyaBraj regionRadha-Krishna traditions and Holi
AlhaBundelkhandHeroic ballads concerning Alha and Udal
Boli or BoliyanPunjabShort folk verses associated with festive occasions and dance

Kajri and Chaiti are distinguished particularly by their seasonal associations. Kajri belongs to the rainy-season repertoire, whereas Chaiti takes its name from Chaitra, which normally falls during March and April.

Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh and Goa

FormRegionDistinctive feature
PowadaMaharashtraHeroic narrative and historical ballads
LavaniMaharashtraExpressive song-and-dance tradition
PaiMadhya PradeshFolk songs associated with seasonal celebrations
DadariaCentral IndiaFolk lyrical songs, often concerning love
MandoGoaSong-and-dance tradition reflecting Goan and Portuguese cultural influences

Powada as a historical ballad

A ballad is a narrative song that relates a story. Powadas celebrate heroic deeds, historical personalities and important events. Several famous Marathi Powadas commemorate Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj and the Maratha struggle.

Such songs preserve historical memories and express the values admired by a community. However, a heroic ballad may contain poetic exaggeration and should not automatically be treated as an exact historical record.

Prelims focus

  • Panihari and Maand belong to Rajasthan.
  • Wanawan is associated with Kashmir.
  • Kajri is a monsoon song, while Chaiti is associated with Chaitra.
  • Alha belongs to the heroic ballad tradition of Bundelkhand.
  • Powada is associated with Maharashtra; Pai with Madhya Pradesh.
  • Trap: Sohar celebrates childbirth; it is not a funeral lament.

[References: IGNOU, BSWE-006, Traditional and Modern Media of Communication, p. 55; IGNOU, Basic Principles and Techniques of Communication, section Folk Oral Literature and Folk Music; Folk Music and Musical Instruments of India Notes, regional folk music entries; NCERT, Our Pasts-II, Class 7, 2020–21, Chapter 9, pp. 122–125; online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Chaiti belongs to spring; Kajri belongs to the monsoon.

title: Regional Folk Music of Northern, Western and Central India

body:
Bengal's riverine and spiritual traditions

The river systems, village life and religious traditions of Bengal have produced several distinctive forms of folk music. Among the best-known are Bhatiali and Baul, which differ in their social setting and principal subject.

Bhatiali

Bhatiali is a traditional riverine folk song associated particularly with boatmen of Bengal, including present-day Bangladesh and West Bengal. Its melodies and themes express the experiences of life on rivers, solitude, longing and separation.

Bhatiali demonstrates how an occupation and a geographical environment can influence a region's musical traditions.

Baul

Bauls are mystic singers of Bengal. Their songs express the search for spiritual truth and the relationship between the individual and the divine. Baul traditions have absorbed influences from Vaishnava Bhakti, Sufism and other spiritual movements while retaining their distinctive identity.

Baul singers are frequently associated with the ektara, a traditional single-string instrument. The dotara and dubki drum are also used. Baul songs are transmitted orally and may serve as a means of spiritual instruction between a teacher and disciple.

Lalon Shah, also known as Lalon Fakir, is a prominent figure associated with the Baul tradition.

Baul and UNESCO recognition

UNESCO inscribed Baul songs on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2008 under Bangladesh. The cultural tradition itself extends across Bangladesh and West Bengal in India. Its geographical distribution must not be confused with the country associated with the UNESCO inscription.

Assam: Bihu songs

Bihu Geet refers to the traditional songs associated with the Bihu festivities of Assam, particularly Rongali or Bohag Bihu.

Rongali Bihu marks the Assamese New Year and the beginning of a new agricultural cycle in spring. Its songs frequently express youth, love, nature and the joy of seasonal renewal. Bihu music is closely associated with instruments such as the dhol, pepa and gogona.

Bihu songs belong primarily to the festive and agricultural folk tradition. They should be distinguished from Borgeet, the devotional compositions associated with the Assamese Vaishnava tradition.

Central and southern narrative music

FormPrincipal regionCharacteristic feature
PandavaniChhattisgarhMusical narration of episodes from the Mahabharata
VillupattuTamil NaduNarrative songs accompanied by a musical bow
BurrakathaAndhra Pradesh and TelanganaStorytelling combining song, narration and dialogue
Kolkali PattuKeralaTraditional songs accompanying Kolkali group performance

Pandavani

The name Pandavani refers to stories of the Pandavas. The performer presents episodes from the Mahabharata through singing and narration. The tradition is particularly associated with Chhattisgarh.

Teejan Bai is one of the most renowned exponents of Pandavani. Her performances helped bring wider recognition to this oral narrative tradition.

Villupattu

Villupattu literally means bow-song. It combines musical narration with the use of a bow-shaped instrument. Its repertoire includes religious stories, legends and subjects of social importance.

Unlike a purely instrumental performance, narrative folk forms depend on intelligible words and stories. Their purpose includes communicating knowledge and preserving collective memory as well as providing entertainment.

Prelims focus

  • Bhatiali is associated with Bengal's boatmen.
  • Baul represents the mystic singing tradition of Bengal.
  • Bihu Geet is a festive folk music tradition of Assam.
  • Pandavani recounts the Mahabharata and is associated with Teejan Bai.
  • Villupattu is a bow-song storytelling tradition of Tamil Nadu.
  • Trap: The UNESCO inscription of Baul songs in 2008 belongs to Bangladesh, although Bauls are also found in India.

[References: UNESCO, Baul Songs, nomination file 00107; IGNOU, BSWE-006, Traditional and Modern Media of Communication, p. 55; National Cultural Audiovisual Archives, Pandavani Performance by Ms. Teejan Bai, recording dated 28 February 1987; Folk Music and Musical Instruments of India Notes, regional traditions; online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: The river environment that shaped Bhatiali songs.

pictures.alt: Four sources of experience shape folk music: rivers and work, Bhatiali; spirituality, Baul; seasonal farming, Bihu Geet; epic memory, Pandavani.

title: Folk Music of Eastern, Northeastern and Southern India

body:
Bhakti and devotional singing

Bhakti means loving devotion to the divine. Although devotional worship has a long history in India, medieval Bhakti movements greatly expanded the use of regional languages, poetry and singing as means of religious expression.

Saint-poets composed verses that ordinary people could understand, remember and sing. These compositions communicated religious teachings without requiring every listener to possess knowledge of Sanskrit or formal religious scholarship.

Saguna and Nirguna Bhakti

Bhakti traditions are commonly classified into 2 broad categories according to their conception of the divine.

AspectSaguna BhaktiNirguna Bhakti
MeaningDevotion to the divine with attributesDevotion to the formless divine
Common themesLove, worship and deeds of a deityInner realization and spiritual unity
ExamplesMirabai, Surdas, Narsinh MehtaKabir, Guru Nanak

This distinction concerns religious belief rather than musical technique. Both Saguna and Nirguna traditions may use devotional songs to communicate their teachings.

Bhajan

A bhajan is a devotional song expressing worship, praise, love, surrender, remembrance or spiritual instruction.

Bhajans may be sung individually or collectively. They commonly use understandable lyrics and memorable melodies. Their themes range from praise of a deity to moral teachings and philosophical reflection.

Mirabai's compositions expressing devotion to Krishna, Narsinh Mehta's devotional songs and the spiritual verses attributed to Kabir illustrate the diversity of the bhajan tradition.

Kirtan

Kirtan is a devotional practice centred on singing or reciting divine names, praises, sacred verses or religious narratives, frequently through collective participation.

In many kirtan traditions, a principal singer introduces a verse or divine name and the assembled devotees repeat or respond to it. This enables participants to take an active part in worship.

Some traditions also combine singing with explanations of religious stories. For example, a kirtankar in Maharashtra may communicate religious and ethical teachings through a combination of narration and devotional songs.

Sankirtan

Sankirtan generally refers to collective devotional singing or chanting. In Vaishnava traditions, it is frequently associated with the repetition of divine names and the narration of Krishna's deeds. Chaitanya Mahaprabhu popularized congregational Krishna devotion through singing and dancing in Bengal.

Distinction between bhajan and kirtan

A bhajan is commonly identified as a devotional song or composition. Kirtan places greater emphasis on the devotional act of singing, chanting or narrating, often as a collective religious practice.

The distinction is not absolute. A bhajan can be sung collectively during a kirtan gathering, and different religious communities use these terms in different ways.

Instruments commonly associated with devotional gatherings

  • Ektara: A traditional single-string instrument associated with folk and devotional singers.
  • Manjira: Small metallic cymbals used to accompany rhythmic singing.
  • Dholak: A drum frequently used in folk and devotional gatherings.
  • Harmonium: A keyboard instrument widely used to accompany modern bhajan and kirtan singing.

No particular instrument is compulsory for every bhajan or kirtan. The instruments and musical arrangements vary according to the tradition and occasion.

Social importance of devotional singing

Devotional gatherings allow people to learn religious teachings through shared participation. Regional-language compositions made the ideas of many saint-poets accessible to artisans, agricultural communities, women and other groups beyond formally educated religious elites.

Many saints used devotional music to question social discrimination, outward displays of piety and excessive dependence on ritual. However, different Bhakti traditions expressed different religious and social positions.

Prelims focus

  • Saguna Bhakti concerns devotion to the divine with attributes.
  • Nirguna Bhakti emphasizes the formless divine.
  • Mirabai and Surdas are associated with Krishna devotion.
  • Kabir emphasized devotion to a formless Supreme Being.
  • Chaitanya Mahaprabhu is associated with congregational Krishna devotion.
  • Trap: Bhajan is not necessarily a solo performance, and every kirtan does not follow an identical musical format.

[References: NCERT, Our Pasts-II, Class 7, 2020–21, Chapter 8, Devotional Paths to the Divine, pp. 104–119; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part II, Class 12, Theme 6, Bhakti-Sufi Traditions, pp. 143–146; NCERT, Living Craft Traditions of India, Class 11, Chapter 10, pp. 117–121; Centre for Cultural Resources and Training, Performing Arts, consulted 26 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: A bhajan is a devotional song that may be sung during kirtan; sankirtan means congregational devotional singing or chanting.
pictures.caption: Bhajan and kirtan are related but not identical.

title: Bhajan, Kirtan and the Musical Expression of Bhakti
